articles.title: Daily briefing: ‘Raygun’ AI can shrink or supersize proteins
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 July 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-02420-9The tool can add, remove or swap protein subunits using similar steps to natural evolution. Plus, spin qubits are back in the quantum race and the drugs that could prevent long COVID.
articles.content:
The tool can add, remove or swap protein subunits using similar steps to natural evolution. Plus, spin qubits are back in the quantum race and the drugs that could prevent long COVID.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

The company HRL Laboratories in Malibu, California, has created a quantum computer that reduces the wiring to its 18 spin qubits to improve performance.Credit: HRL Laboratories

Four independent research teams have reported big advances in the design of quantum devices that rely on ‘spin qubits’ to encode information. Spin qubits are made by carving precise patterns into semiconductor wafers, forming wells that can hold a single electron. In the race to create a useful quantum computer, this design had previously not been considered a front-runner, because systems that used spin qubits were small and had high error rates. The new systems range from 5 to 18 qubits, and one has slashed the error rate to less than 0.01%.

Nature | 6 min read

Reference: Nature paper 1 & paper 2 and arXiv preprint 1 & preprint 2 (not peer reviewed)

An artificial-intelligence tool dubbed ‘Raygun’ can miniaturize or supersize a natural protein without disrupting the protein’s shape or ability to function. Raygun can modify existing proteins, using some of the same steps as natural evolution: adding or deleting single protein subunits or substituting one protein subunit for another. Raygun can make “exactly what researchers want — not a completely new protein, but a better, smaller, larger or more adaptable version of one they already trust,” says computational biologist Fajie Yuan.

Nature | 4 min read

Reference: Nature paper

The results of rigorous clinical trials suggest that two drugs can prevent an infection with COVID-19 from developing into long COVID, a chronic condition characterized by fatigue and cognitive impairment. The first trial reported that paxlovid, an antiviral COVID-19 treatment, reduced the risk of long COVID developing after three months by 40%. Another reports that the diabetes drug metformin reduces the risk of long COVID at six months after infection by around half. The trial results have divided physicians — some think the results are promising enough to start prescribing the drugs for this purpose; others disagree.

Nature | 6 min read

Reference: The Lancet Infectious Diseases paper & Clinical Infectious Diseases paper

Infographic of the week

Source: Ref. 2

Disease-carrying mosquitoes have now spread to previously unaffected regions in Europe, Asia, the Americas and Australia. Climate change has made some regions more suitable for mosquitoes than they were, with warm temperatures and rain extending over longer periods of the year giving the insects more time to get established and spread disease. Live mosquitoes can also travel on cars, trains and planes, covering long distances in just a few hours, so the expansion of global trade routes has also enabled the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. (Nature | 6 min read)

Features & opinion

Without an available vaccine or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola spreading in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), controlling the outbreak relies on identifying and isolating cases. These measures can’t succeed without public trust, but efforts to build it aren’t considered a core public health intervention, argue a group of public-health researchers. The DRC, and other countries affected by Ebola, must plan and finance social and behavioural change programs “as a core pillar of outbreak preparedness and response, not as a communications add-on”, the group writes.

Nature Africa | 5 min read

Since the 1990s, communities across Nepal have successfully led efforts to restore large areas of forest land in the country — and with it, habitats for predators such as leopards (Panthera pardus). The reintroduction of these carnivores is a conservation success, but their proximity to villages has led to attacks on people and livestock. Protections such as spiked collars for farm animals and strong fences could lessen the frequency of such encounters, researchers suggest. But programs that provide financial compensation are key to defuse tension between residents and their new neighbours, they say.

Knowable | 7 min read

Social-justice campaigner Mary Gray uses her background as a statistician to fight human-rights abuses. Her pursuit of law in the 1970s, after obtaining a PhD in mathematics, was fuelled by the inequitable retirement benefits for men and women. Since then, she’s worked to combat workplace discrimination in the United States, and led projects to combat human-rights violations in the wake of the genocide in Rwanda. “If you think something is important, stick with it yourself, work hard and try to enlist others,” she says.

Nature | 9 min read
articles.reasoning: The article highlights significant advances in AI-driven protein engineering that can create improved versions of natural proteins, potentially accelerating biomedical research and therapeutic development. It also reports promising clinical trial results showing that existing drugs can reduce the risk of long COVID, a condition affecting millions globally. These developments have broad positive implications for health and medicine, with clear, substantive impact described.

articles.title: Climate change may help eliminate malaria from West and Central Africa
articles.summary: Global warming may make it too hot for malaria-carrying mosquitoes to survive in parts of Africa, but could also shift the problem to less affected areas
articles.content:
Global warming may make it too hot for malaria-carrying mosquitoes to survive in parts of Africa, but could also shift the problem to less affected areas

Malari-prevention strategies like bed nets are crucial in the fight against the infection Hajarah Nalwadda/Getty Images

By the end of this century, malaria could be eradicated in West and Central Africa, two of the worst-affected regions. A modelling study suggests cases will plummet in these areas if the extreme heat caused by climate change makes them uninhabitable for mosquitoes. But this also means malaria is expected to become more pronounced in the cooler regions of Africa.

“The overall story is that the burden is shifting,” says Tamma Carleton at the University of California, Berkeley.

Climate change is generally associated with worsening infections, as animals like mosquitoes start thriving in regions that were previously too cool for them. But in some cases, excessive heat means the insects can no longer survive in their original habitats.

Advertisement

Malaria, which caused an estimated 610,000 deaths in 80 countries in 2024, occurs when people get bitten by a mosquito infected by a Plasmodium parasite. Laboratory tests indicate the ideal temperature for mosquito survival and parasitic development is between 16°C and 34°C, with malarial transmission highest at 26°C.

Now, Carleton and her colleagues have analysed data published in 2017, which includes information from more than 50,000 surveys of malaria prevalence across sub-Saharan Africa between 1900 and 2016. They have condensed this data into 9875 monthly averages at state or province level, and used different climate simulations to estimate how human-led global warming influenced malaria infections over this time period.

Their results suggest that from 2010 to 2014, human-caused climate change resulted in an additional 1 child per 1000 developing malaria across sub-Saharan Africa, compared with what would have been expected during those years without this warming. These additional infections were most concentrated in West and Central Africa.

Free newsletter Sign up to Health Check Sign up to newsletter

Next, the researchers projected future impacts by running the same models under low, intermediate and high greenhouse gas emissions scenarios. Their results suggest that under high emissions – which would lead to about a 2.4 degree Celsius rise in global temperatures – there could be around 45 fewer children per 1000 with malaria in West Africa by 2100, compared with 2015 to 2020. Central African nations like the Democratic Republic of the Congo, meanwhile, could have 16 fewer cases per 1000.

This – combined with existing malaria prevention strategies like vaccines, insecticides and bed nets – may help eradicate the condition from these areas, says Carleton.

But the team’s results also suggest that malaria prevalence will rise in cooler or high-elevation areas, including parts of Kenya, Burundi, Angola, Zambia and northeastern South Africa. These areas have had less investment in malaria prevention strategies, says Carleton. They will probably also have fewer people with acquired immunity to these parasites.

“This is a meticulous paper that leverages good new data,” says Ilan Noy at Victoria University of Wellington in New Zealand. “Ultimately, however, it finds that climate is only of second-order effect in determining malaria prevalence. By far more important are public health investments. Elimination requires a functioning health system so infected individuals do not continue the chain [of transmission].”

Global efforts to reduce emissions could curb these regional rises in cases, says Carlton. “The blessing, or curse, with CO2 is that abating a ton of CO2 has the same impact on the global climate, no matter where you do it,” she says. “So, whether we’re curbing emissions in Beijing or New York, we have the potential to generate benefits, particularly for Africa and parts of the Global South.”

Sadie Ryan at the University of Florida says this “really elegant study” pulls together various types of data to project the impacts of climate change. “Overall, it’s sad to see such stark evidence of climate-driven shifts”, especially given our capacity to mitigate this, she says.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant and hopeful scientific projection that climate change may lead to the eradication of malaria in West and Central Africa by making these regions too hot for mosquitoes to survive. This represents a potentially large-scale positive impact on public health in some of the worst-affected areas. The story is focused on this single, well-supported topic with detailed data and modeling results, highlighting a tangible future benefit while acknowledging challenges elsewhere. It also emphasizes the importance of continued public health efforts and global emissions reductions, making it a nuanced and inspiring good news story.

articles.title: Somatic mutations reveal the ontogeny of microglia in human aging
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 30 July 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10939-0Somatic mutations reveal the ontogeny of microglia in human aging
articles.content: Microglia are the resident macrophages of the central nervous system1. In mice, microglia seed the brain during embryogenesis and can be maintained throughout life with minimal input from adult hematopoiesis2-4. The origins of human microglia are less clear, but recent evidence suggests that marrow-derived cells contribute to the human microglial pool in certain individuals5-9. Here, to investigate the ontogeny of human microglia, we develop an approach that uses the collection of accumulated somatic mutations which uniquely labels each clone of cells to track the infiltration of marrow-derived cells into the human brain. Applying this approach to 20 aged individuals, we find evidence of an influx of marrow-derived cells into the brain in all examined individuals. Single cell analysis, including single cell lineage tracing using mitochondrial DNA variants, demonstrates that these infiltrating cells are similar to microglia and can comprise a large fraction of the microglial pool. Analysis of human cohort data demonstrates a protective association between most types of clonal hematopoiesis and Alzheimer’s disease. In sum, this work uncovers a widespread influx of myeloid cells into the healthy human brain which contributes to the pool of human microglia and becomes common with aging.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery about the origins and dynamics of microglia in the aging human brain, revealing marrow-derived cells contribute substantially to the microglial pool. This insight has broad implications for understanding brain aging and diseases like Alzheimer's, potentially guiding future therapies and improving health outcomes for the aging population.
articles.personality_title: New study uncovers how bone marrow cells join brain’s immune system with age
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Microglia are special immune cells living in the brain that help protect it. In mice, scientists know these cells come from early development and stay in the brain for life. But in humans, it was unclear if new microglia come from other parts of the body as people get older.

**What happened** – Researchers studied brain cells from 20 older people. They used a method that tracks tiny changes in DNA called somatic mutations to follow where the cells came from. They found that bone marrow cells, which make blood and immune cells, enter the brain and become microglia. These new microglia from bone marrow made up a large part of the brain’s microglial cells in older adults.

**Impact** – This discovery shows that the brain’s immune system changes with age by adding new cells from the bone marrow. It also found a link between these new cells and protection against Alzheimer’s disease, a common brain illness in older people. Understanding this could help scientists find new ways to keep brains healthy as people age.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to learn more about how these bone marrow cells help the brain and how they might be used to treat or prevent brain diseases like Alzheimer’s. They will study how these cells work and how to encourage their positive effects.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Bone marrow cells join the brain’s immune system as we age, offering new clues to protect brain health and fight diseases like Alzheimer’s.

articles.title: Could eating less protein slow ageing?
articles.summary: Protein is everywhere, but studies – mostly in non-human animals – suggest that limiting our intake could extend our lifespan
articles.content:
Protein is everywhere, but studies – mostly in non-human animals – suggest that limiting our intake could extend our lifespan

Protein is an essential nutrient, but can you have too much of a good thing? Anja Burgar/Getty Images

Protein-rich products – from cereal to crisps to coffee – are all over supermarket shelves, but mounting evidence in non-human animals suggests that restricting our intake could slow ageing and extend lifespan. So, does that mean eating too much protein is harmful?

“We have this impression that dietary protein is sort of a universally good thing,” says Dudley Lamming at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. But according to the latest review of the evidence, “increasing dietary protein, beyond what’s needed, for sedentary individuals or animals leads to metabolic problems and can lead to shorter lifespan as well”, he says.

But others point out that nutritional studies in animals like mice and rats don’t readily translate to people, and a high protein intake has been linked to benefits in humans.

Advertisement

Lamming and his colleagues sifted through more than 300 studies, mostly in sedentary rodents, that explored how restricting protein intake to the minimum required to prevent deficiency affects ageing and lifespan.

In these studies, rodents generally either ate the equivalent of the minimum protein requirement recommended by US guidelines – 0.8 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight – or about double that. The latter is similar to the intake recently recommended by US dietary guidelines for optimal health, 1.2 to 1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight.

In one study, rats that ate around the minimum protein intake lived nearly 120 days, or more than 50 per cent, longer than those that ate about double that.

This may be because protein restriction increases levels of the hormone FGF21, says Lamming. In rodents, this acts on the brain, fat tissue and the liver to improve blood sugar levels and reduce the number of senescent cells. These cells, which accumulate with age, have stopped dividing and cause chronic inflammation.

Restricting protein intake has also been shown to dampen the activity of a protein called mTORC1 in mice. mTORC1 ordinarily stimulates cell growth, but reducing its activity boosts cellular repair. “It essentially switches cells from a proliferative state, where they’re growing and engaging a lot of metabolism, to one where they’re dividing more slowly, if at all, and focusing on repair,” says Lamming. Studies suggest this cuts the risk of age-related conditions and extends lifespan in mice, he says.

All this suggests that the recent trend to up our protein intake is probably fine among people who exercise regularly, because they may need more protein to repair muscle damage, but eating more than is needed could cause harm in sedentary individuals, says Lamming.

But Donald Layman at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign points out that rodents vary hugely from people when it comes to protein metabolism. For instance, mTORC1 is activated by feeding, and while people tend to a have a few big meals a day, rodents graze more regularly. Protein restriction may therefore affect mTORC1 pathways differently between the different species, he says. We are also more exposed to factors that accelerate ageing, like infections and extreme heat, than lab animals, says Layman.

What’s more, the review does not include most of the studies in people that suggest that upping our protein intake beyond the minimum cuts our risk of frailty, he says.

Dudley says no studies were intentionally omitted. “We were focused on protein restriction, not the many studies looking at higher levels of protein intake,” he says. Beyond building muscle and preventing frailty, there’s mixed evidence on whether a higher protein intake helps with ageing, says Dudley.

For instance, one study linked this to a reduced risk of age-related muscle loss, or sarcopenia, among older twins in the UK. But the rates of sarcopenia were so low that the link is unreliable, says Elizabeth Williams at the University of Sheffield in the UK.

Still, some studies showed that restricting intake of certain amino acids – such as isoleucine and valine, which are highest in meat, fish and dairy – in mice has a similar effect to limiting overall protein intake, says Philip Atherton at Nottingham University, UK.

Atherton says he is planning a study to investigate whether drugs that deplete specific amino acids in people improve outcomes like blood sugar control, with results expected in the next few years.

articles.personality_title: New research explores how eating less protein might slow aging
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Protein is an important nutrient found in many foods, but recent studies mostly in animals suggest that eating less protein could help animals live longer and age more slowly. Scientists are now looking at whether this could also apply to people.

**What happened** – Researchers reviewed over 300 studies on rodents that compared low protein diets to higher protein diets. They found that rodents eating just the minimum protein needed lived about 50% longer than those eating double that amount. Scientists think this may be because eating less protein changes certain hormones and cell activities that help the body repair itself and reduce harmful aging effects.

**Impact** – This research challenges the common idea that more protein is always better, especially for people who do not exercise much. It suggests that eating more protein than needed might cause health problems and shorten lifespan for some. However, experts warn that what happens in animals may not work the same way in humans, because people and rodents process protein differently.

**What's next step** – Scientists plan to study whether limiting specific parts of protein, called amino acids, can help people live healthier lives. Some are also testing new drugs that might target these amino acids to improve health, with results expected in a few years.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Studies in animals show that eating just enough protein may help slow aging, but more research is needed to understand how this applies to people.
articles.personality_title_fr: De nouvelles recherches explorent comment manger moins de protéines pourrait ralentir le vieillissement
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les protéines sont un nutriment important présent dans de nombreux aliments. Des études récentes, principalement sur des animaux, suggèrent que manger moins de protéines pourrait aider ces animaux à vivre plus longtemps et à vieillir plus lentement. Les scientifiques cherchent maintenant à savoir si cela pourrait aussi s'appliquer aux humains.

**Ce qui s'est passé** – Des chercheurs ont examiné plus de 300 études sur des rongeurs comparant des régimes pauvres en protéines à des régimes plus riches. Ils ont découvert que les rongeurs qui mangeaient juste la quantité minimale de protéines vivaient environ 50 % plus longtemps que ceux qui en mangeaient le double. Les scientifiques pensent que cela s'explique par des changements dans certaines hormones et activités cellulaires qui aident le corps à se réparer et à réduire les effets nocifs du vieillissement.

**Impact** – Cette recherche remet en question l'idée courante selon laquelle plus de protéines est toujours mieux, surtout pour les personnes peu actives. Elle suggère que manger plus de protéines que nécessaire pourrait causer des problèmes de santé et raccourcir la durée de vie chez certains. Cependant, les experts avertissent que ce qui se passe chez les animaux ne fonctionne pas forcément de la même manière chez les humains, car le métabolisme des protéines est différent.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques prévoient d'étudier si limiter certains composants des protéines, appelés acides aminés, peut aider les gens à vivre en meilleure santé. Certains testent aussi de nouveaux médicaments ciblant ces acides aminés pour améliorer la santé, avec des résultats attendus dans quelques années.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Des études sur les animaux montrent que manger juste assez de protéines pourrait ralentir le vieillissement, mais il faut encore des recherches pour comprendre comment cela s'applique aux humains.
articles.personality_title_es: Nuevas investigaciones exploran cómo comer menos proteínas podría ralentizar el envejecimiento
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Las proteínas son un nutriente importante que se encuentra en muchos alimentos, pero estudios recientes, principalmente en animales, sugieren que comer menos proteínas podría ayudar a los animales a vivir más tiempo y envejecer más lentamente. Los científicos ahora están investigando si esto también podría aplicarse a las personas.

**Qué pasó** – Investigadores revisaron más de 300 estudios en roedores que compararon dietas bajas en proteínas con dietas altas en proteínas. Encontraron que los roedores que consumían solo la cantidad mínima necesaria de proteínas vivían aproximadamente un 50 % más que los que consumían el doble. Los científicos creen que esto puede deberse a que comer menos proteínas cambia ciertas hormonas y actividades celulares que ayudan al cuerpo a repararse y reducir los efectos dañinos del envejecimiento.

**Impacto** – Esta investigación cuestiona la idea común de que más proteínas siempre es mejor, especialmente para las personas que no hacen mucho ejercicio. Sugiere que consumir más proteínas de las necesarias podría causar problemas de salud y acortar la vida útil en algunos casos. Sin embargo, los expertos advierten que lo que ocurre en animales puede no funcionar igual en humanos, porque las personas y los roedores procesan las proteínas de manera diferente.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos planean estudiar si limitar ciertas partes de las proteínas, llamadas aminoácidos, puede ayudar a las personas a vivir vidas más saludables. Algunos también están probando nuevos medicamentos que podrían dirigir estos aminoácidos para mejorar la salud, con resultados esperados en unos años.

**Resumen en una frase** – Estudios en animales muestran que comer solo la cantidad necesaria de proteínas puede ayudar a ralentizar el envejecimiento, pero se necesita más investigación para entender cómo se aplica esto a las personas.
